title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent with command execution access wiped a production database when a migration command intended for a test environment was pointed at production credentials instead. The agent had no access restrictions and was connected directly to a live Supabase database. Nothing in the command syntax flagged the danger to the system before execution.

Two control failures made this possible. The deployment lacked a policy validation layer to block commands targeting production resources before they run. The database credentials also lacked scope limitations that would have restricted the agent to non-production environments only. A developer instructed the agent to fix schema issues without these safeguards in place.

It is not established how the command's target was misconfigured, whether by the agent's reasoning or the developer's setup. The incident shows that systems giving AI agents command execution should treat destructive errors as inevitable and require approval gates before irreversible operations, not rely on discovering damage afterward.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In August 2026, a developer connected an AI coding agent running Claude Opus 5 to a production Supabase database without access restrictions. While instructing the agent to analyze and fix database schema issues, a Prisma migration command intended for a test database was accidentally pointed at the production database URL instead. The agent executed the command, which reset and emptied all production tables within approximately ten minutes. The agent detected the error and reported it to the developer before the developer noticed the problem themselves.

The incident occurred because nothing in the command's syntax indicated danger, and the database credentials lacked scope limitations. Two controls could have prevented the disaster: a policy validation layer that checks whether commands target production resources before execution, and scoped credentials that would have restricted the agent's access to non-production environments only. The article emphasizes that any agent with command execution access will eventually issue an incorrect command, making safeguard systems essential rather than relying on discovering damage after the fact.
